text:
A nuclear reactor generates heat through controlled nuclear fission. Fuel rods containing enriched uranium-235 absorb neutrons, causing their nuclei to split. This splits the uranium atom, releasing massive amounts of heat energy and additional free neutrons. These new neutrons strike other uranium atoms, creating a self-sustaining chain reaction.

Control rods made of neutron-absorbing materials (like boron or cadmium) regulate the reaction rate by inserting deeper to slow it down or withdrawing to speed it up. The heat generated boils water into high-pressure steam, which drives turbines connected to generators, producing electricity. Coolant systems circulate water to remove heat from the core and prevent overheating. After passing through the turbine, steam is condensed back into water and recycled. The entire process is enclosed in a robust containment building to ensure safety.
